title: AP Statistics
summary: Use the revised five-unit sequence to study design, probability, inference and regression.
frameworkNote: Unit map checked against College Board on 15 October 2026 for the 2026-27 course. Each unit has one focused original revision lesson, not exhaustive topic coverage or an official practice paper. Uses the Fall 2026 five-unit revision, confirmed at https://apcentral.collegeboard.org/courses/ap-statistics/future-revisions. Historical nine-unit numbering is not used; removed slope-inference and goodness-of-fit topics are not presented as current requirements.

modules.title: Design a comparison before collecting data
modules.focus: Match an investigative question to a sampling or experimental design.
explanation: A useful statistical question identifies a population, variables and anticipated variation. A random sample supports generalisation to its sampling population. Random assignment creates treatment groups with a basis for a causal comparison; these two randomisation steps do different jobs.

Describe quantitative distributions using shape, centre, spread and unusual observations. Median and interquartile range resist extreme values better than mean and standard deviation. A summary must name the variable and its units, not merely list calculations.

workedExample.prompt: A school randomly assigns 60 volunteers to two study methods. What can the design support?
steps: Random assignment permits a causal comparison of the methods for participants, subject to execution and uncertainty.
Volunteering limits generalisation; assignment does not turn the volunteers into a random sample of all pupils.

misconception.claim: Random assignment automatically makes a sample representative.
misconception.correction: It balances treatment allocation in expectation, not selection into the study.

questions.prompt: For times 2,3,3,4,18 minutes, find the mean and median.
questions.hint: Sort the values and compare sensitivity to 18.

questions.prompt: A survey samples only library visitors to estimate all pupils’ reading habits. Identify a limitation.
questions.hint: Compare the sampling frame with the population.
questions.answer: Undercoverage: pupils who do not visit the library cannot be selected.
checkpoints: Explain how its habits may differ.

modules.title: Conditional probability and repeated trials
modules.focus: Choose the denominator from the condition.
explanation: Conditional probability P(A|B) measures the fraction of B outcomes that also satisfy A. Independence requires P(A|B)=P(A), when defined. Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so nonzero mutually exclusive events are not independent.

A binomial count requires a fixed number of independent trials, two outcomes per trial and a constant success probability. Its mean is np and standard deviation √(np(1-p)). Check the modelling conditions before applying a formula.

workedExample.prompt: Among 40 club members, 16 cycle; 10 of the 16 cyclists wear helmets. Find P(helmet|cycles).
steps: The condition restricts the denominator to 16 cyclists.

misconception.correction: The two probabilities usually have different conditioning groups and denominators.

questions.prompt: Four independent trials have success probability 0.5. Find P(exactly 3 successes).
questions.hint: Count the four possible failure positions.

questions.prompt: A binomial count has n=100 and p=0.2. Find its mean and standard deviation.
checkpoints: Take the square root for standard deviation.

modules.title: Estimating a population proportion
modules.focus: Interpret an interval as a method with repeated-sample coverage.
explanation: For a random sample, a large-sample confidence interval for one population proportion is p̂±z*√(p̂(1-p̂)/n). Check independence and sufficiently many observed successes and failures before using the normal approximation.

A confidence level describes how often the procedure captures the fixed population proportion across repeated samples. It is not the percentage of people inside the interval. Significance tests instead assess how unusual sample evidence would be under a stated null proportion.

workedExample.prompt: In a random sample of 400 pupils from a much larger population, 240 prefer a schedule. Use z*=1.96 for an approximate 95% interval.
steps: p̂=0.6 and standard error=√(0.6·0.4/400)≈0.02449; both observed counts exceed 10.

misconception.claim: A 95% interval contains 95% of individual responses.
misconception.correction: It estimates a population proportion, not a range of individual outcomes.

questions.prompt: If sample size quadruples with the same p̂ and confidence level, what happens to the margin of error?
questions.hint: Track the square root of n.

questions.prompt: A test has p-value 0.03 and α=0.05. State the decision, without claiming certainty.
questions.answer: Reject the null; the evidence is statistically significant at 0.05.
checkpoints: Rejection does not prove the alternative with certainty.

modules.title: Inference for a mean and paired change
modules.focus: Match the analysis to how observations were collected.
explanation: When a population standard deviation is unknown, inference for a mean uses the sample standard deviation and a t distribution. For one mean, the standard error is s/√n and degrees of freedom are n-1.

For before-and-after observations on the same people, analyse within-person differences rather than treating the groups as independent. Randomisation, independence between sampled units and a suitable shape or adequate sample size remain conditions, not optional decorations.

workedExample.prompt: A random sample of 25 independent changes has mean 4 and standard deviation 10. Using t*=2.064, calculate a confidence interval for the population mean change; assume the shape condition holds.

misconception.claim: Paired data should always be analysed as two independent samples.
misconception.correction: Pairing links the observations; analyse the differences to preserve that structure.

questions.prompt: For n=36, sample mean 18, s=6 and null mean 16, find the one-sample t statistic.
questions.hint: Divide the mean difference by s/√n.

questions.prompt: An interval for mean change is (-1.2,3.4). Does it exclude no average change?
questions.answer: No. Zero lies within the interval.
checkpoints: Use the interval for the population mean.
Do not conclude every participant had zero change.

modules.title: Regression predictions and residuals
modules.focus: Measure an observation’s distance from its fitted prediction.
explanation: A least-squares line predicts a response from an explanatory variable by minimising squared vertical residuals. A residual equals observed response minus predicted response. A positive residual means the observation lies above the fitted line.

Correlation describes linear association and has no units. It does not establish causation. Prediction far beyond the observed input range is extrapolation and needs separate justification. A slope must be interpreted in response units per explanatory-variable unit.

workedExample.prompt: A model predicts reading time ŷ=12+3x minutes for x pages. A four-page reading takes 27 minutes. Find the residual.
steps: Residual=27-24=3 minutes, so the observed time is above the prediction.

misconception.claim: A strong correlation proves that changing x causes y to change.
misconception.correction: Confounding and study design still determine whether a causal conclusion is justified.

questions.prompt: For ŷ=8-0.5x, predict y at x=6.
A line is fitted using ages 12–18. Is predicting at age 60 interpolation?
checkpoints: The relationship may change outside that range.
